Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette:
Meena was a 61-year-old South Asian woman who had worked most of her life in agricultural fields with her husband, rising before dawn to tend crops and moving through the day with the rhythm of the land. The rape occurred many years earlier, on a stretch of ground she knew well, while she was working alone and had briefly been separated from the others. What stayed with her was not only the assault itself but the way ordinary things around it had become charged afterward: a dog barking sharply near the field edge could make her chest tighten at once, and any unexpected brush against her body could send her flinching before she had even understood what had happened. Even now, when she described it, she spoke as if her body had learned to anticipate danger faster than her mind could catch up, and she had come to believe that the world could turn unsafe in an instant without warning.

In the months after the assault, Meena began to notice that memories did not arrive like ordinary recollections. They came on suddenly, triggered by a sight, a sound, or a feeling in her surroundings that she could not always predict, and when they did she was pulled straight back into the event. She said that her memories of the frightening event were like a film playing over and over, with the same scenes looping through her mind despite her efforts to push them away. At times she would be standing in the kitchen, hearing a dog in the lane outside, and the whole memory would rush in with such force that she felt as if it were happening right then. Sexual situations or even the suggestion of intimacy with her husband could produce the same immediate jolt, not because she wanted to dwell on the past, but because those moments seemed to open the door to the memory without any warning at all.

Meena’s sleep slowly became tied to that sense of danger. She lay awake at night trying to stay alert, telling herself she could not fully let go because she might miss something important if she did. In bed she listened for movement outside the house and for any sudden noise that might require her to react, and she often felt uneasy when her husband shifted and touched her unexpectedly, as though the touch itself were a threat. Her body reacted before she had time to think, and that startled response deepened her conviction that she had to remain watchful. The more she noticed her own alarm, the more certain she became that she was not truly safe, even in the familiar rooms of her home.

Over the years, these experiences narrowed her life. She became hesitant about walking near stray dogs on the way to the fields and increasingly uneasy when work brought her close to places that reminded her of being alone outdoors. At home, she kept her distance during moments of closeness, and her husband noticed that she grew tense if he came up behind her or touched her without notice. Meena did not describe this as fear in so many words; rather, she explained it as necessity, something she had to do to avoid being overtaken by the same horror again. Yet every time a trigger appeared in her daily environment, her vigilance sharpened, her body braced, and the old memory seemed to arrive with renewed force, making it harder for her to rest or feel present in her own life.

By the time she sought help, Meena was exhausted by the constant effort of staying ready. She said she finally came because she was tired of living as though danger were always just outside the door, and because she no longer wanted her nights to be ruled by fear of sleep or her days by sudden surges of memory. What frightened her most was the sense that one unexpected dog bark, one accidental touch, or one moment of intimacy could still carry her back into the assault without warning; what she hoped for, more quietly, was to be able to lie down at night and feel, at least sometimes, that she was in the present rather than trapped in the past.
